title: Are Appliance Extended Warranties Worth It?
summary: Appliance retailers who back and service their own extended warranty pitch it as better than resold third-party contracts, while laying out when a warranty actually pays off.

assertions.quote: They have to get authorization every single time, and it's very misleading.

verdicts.note: Third-party backed contracts do route approvals through the backer, which can add friction, but it does not mean coverage is routinely denied — it varies by backer and plan.

assertions.quote: It's as good as this piece of paper, really, in earnest because they don't have the autonomy to make the decision in the moment

verdicts.note: This is generally true structurally for most reseller arrangements, though some third-party administrators still grant sellers claims-adjudication authority.

assertions.quote: If you never have to make a claim on extended warranty portion of that service, you get half of that back
Seven, eight, nine, and ten year warranties don't really exist.

verdicts.note: This overstates the case — some reputable manufacturer and dealer plans do offer and honor longer terms, so blanket non-honoring is not universal.

assertions.quote: it is inclusive of the manufacturer warranty, not on top of.

verdicts.note: This matches how most extended service contracts are structured — the term runs from the original delivery date, overlapping rather than stacking with factory coverage.

assertions.quote: The warranty is transferable. So as long as you don't move that warranty, without a plan.
service generally happens in the first sixty, ninety one year of warranty

verdicts.note: Appliance failure-rate data does show a bathtub-curve pattern with early infant-mortality and later wear-out failures, though exact timing varies by product and brand.
